To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we observe and measure inelastic atom-molecule and molecule-molecule collision rates of approximately 2-3 times 10(-11 cm3 s(-l)) for Cs and Cs2, respectively, in an optical dipole trap.
inelastic atom-molecule and molecule-molecule collision rates are measured inside a CO2-laser-dipole trap, with rates comparable to the ones observed in magnetic traps.
inelastic atom-molecule collision rate coefficients of approximately 2-3 x 10(-10) cm3 s-1 are measured for cold cesium atoms and molecules confined in an optical trap.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel technique to produce cold molecules, based on the combination of an optical dipole trap with a magneto-optical trap (MOT) for the production of a pure sample of cold molecules, and a magnetic trap for the production of cold atoms.
the investigation of the inelastic atom-molecule and molecule-molecule collisions, and the lifetime of a pure molecular sample in an optical trap.
the investigation of cold inelastic atom-molecule collisional processes in a dipole trap.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in a dipole trap, atom-molecule collisions are the dominant inelastic process.
the atom-molecule inelastic collisions are the limiting process in the lifetime of an atom-molecule mixture.
the inelastic atom-molecule and molecule-molecule collision rates are comparable to the elastic ones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the inelastic atom-molecule rate is approximately 10(-9) times smaller than the elastic rate and approximately 100 times larger than the inelastic molecule molecule rate.
the lifetime of the molecule sample is limited by the molecule-molecule inelastic collision, while the lifetime of the atom sample is limited by atom-molecule inelastic collisions.
we are able to observe and measure cold inelastic atom-molecule and molecule-molecule collisions in the presence of a CO2 laser beam.
The main takeaway from our work is that

inelastic atom-molecule collision rates can be measured and controlled with a high degree of precision in a laser dipole trap, and that the trap lifetime is mainly limited by rest gas atoms and molecules.
the atom-molecule collisions are the dominant loss mechanism in an optically confined atomic and molecular sample, even at temperatures as low as 10 mK.
inelastic collisions between atoms and molecules in a CO2 laser trap are not negligible.
